title: Where is the bank?
title_target: ဘဏ် ဘယ်မှာ ရှိလဲ — baⁿ bè-hma shee.-lè:
goal: Ask where things are and give directions, and get used to the Burmese habit of putting prepositions after the noun — including words like "inside", "next to", and "in front of".
bekal: ask where something is with ဘယ်မှာ ရှိလဲ
use မှာ for every expression of place
describe position with ထဲမှာ, ဘေးမှာ, ရှေ့မှာ, နောက်မှာ
say near, far, and on the left or right

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — Asking the way in the street
dialogs.intro: Ani needs to go to the bank and asks a roadside tea seller. Notice that every place expression uses the same single marker, မှာ, and that it always comes **after** the name of the place.

grammars.title: ⚠️ မှာ closes every expression of place
body: English has many prepositions: at, in, on, inside. Burmese has only one place marker, မှာ (*hma*), and it always goes **after** the name of the place. Finer distinctions like "inside", "in front of", and "next to" are expressed by extra words inserted **before** မှာ.

head: Burmese
Say it
Literal translation
Meaning
rows: အိမ် ထဲမှာ
အိမ် ဘေးမှာ
အိမ် နောက်မှာ
အိမ် အပေါ်မှာ
အိမ် အောက်မှာ

after: Notice that the order is always **the big place first, then the part**: "house — inside — at", not "inside — house — at". Burmese always moves from big to small, and that habit will show up again in addresses, dates, and times.

grammars.title: ရှိတယ် for location, once again
body: The same verb you used for "have" in unit 4 is also used for "be located". The sentence order: place first, the thing, then ရှိတယ် at the end.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: ဘဏ် ဘယ်မှာ ရှိလဲ
it's in front of the market
ဒီနားမှာ မရှိဘူး
အိမ်မှာ ဘယ်သူ ရှိလဲ

after: ⚠️ For **people**, many speakers use either ရှိတယ် or နေတယ် ("live, stay"): အဖေ အိမ်မှာ ရှိတယ် and အဖေ အိမ်မှာ နေတယ် are both correct. For **things**, only ရှိတယ် is used.

grammars.title: …ရင် — if
body: ရင် (*yiⁿ*) attaches after a verb and means "if" or "when". The if-clause always comes **first** — in English you can say "I won't go if it rains", but Burmese only allows "if it rains, I won't go".

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: လမ်းလျှောက်ရင် ငါးမိနစ်ပဲ
if you walk, it's only five minutes
အားရင် လာပါ
if it rains, I won't go
နှစ်ထည်ဆို ဈေးပေါတယ်

after: ဆို (*hsoh*) is used in a similar way, but it suits conditions that are **a thing or an amount** rather than an action — like "if it's two (longyis)" in unit 6's dialogue. For actions, use ရင်.

grammars.title: Near, far, and the polite opener
body: One phrase to learn whole today: **တစ်ဆိတ်လောက်** (*ta.hsayk-lowk*), meaning "excuse me a moment". It opens almost every question you'll ask a stranger in the street.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: တစ်ဆိတ်လောက်
ဘယ်ဘက် · ညာဘက်
on the left · on the right
နားလည်ပါပြီ

after: နားလည်တယ် literally means "the ear takes it in" — a very vivid picture for "understand". If you **don't** understand, say နားမလည်ဘူး (*na:-ma.lè-boo:*), and people will repeat it more slowly without the slightest annoyance.

blocks.text: This list covers everyday errands in any town in Myanmar. Notice that many places are formed by attaching ဆိုင် ("shop") or ရုံ ("building") to a root word — once you see the pattern, the number of words to memorize drops by half.

blocks.title: Asking the way without getting lost
items: Open with **တစ်ဆိတ်လောက်** and then a respectful title: ဦးလေး for a man, အဒေါ် for a woman. Those two words are enough to make people stop and help.

⚠️ If the answer is too fast, don't nod politely and walk off — say **နားမလည်ဘူး၊ ဖြေးဖြေး ပြောပါဦး** (*na:-ma.lè-boo:, hpyay:-hpyay: pyò:-ba-ohⁿ:*), "I don't understand, please speak slowly". It's the most valuable sentence in this whole book.
People in Myanmar often point with their **chin or lips**, not their index finger. If the person seems to nod toward one side, that's the direction — not a meaningless gesture.
